text: The Italian Communist Party (PCI), originally founded as the Communist Party of Italy (PCd'I) on 21 January 1921 in Livorno, seceded from the Italian Socialist Party (PSI) following a split at the XVII Congress of the PSI, which refused to expel reformist elements as required by the Communist International (Comintern). The new party was led by Amadeo Bordiga, Antonio Gramsci, and Nicola Bombacci, with Bordiga elected secretary. The PCd'I began as a territorial section of the Comintern, adopting its program and tactics from the II Congress of the Moscow Bolsheviks, including a ten-point program that criticized capitalism and called for the extinction of the state. In 1922, the party registered 43,000 members, partly due to the entry of the Socialist Youth Federation, and established a Central Committee of 15 members, including five in the Executive Committee. The party emphasized forming a society hostile to bourgeois structures, with Bordiga initially seen as the leading figure, while Gramsci and Angelo Tasca represented center and right factions. In 1923, members were arrested for "conspiracy against the State," and by 1924–1925, the Comintern launched a campaign of Bolshevisation, consolidating control in favor of the center, which aligned with Moscow. The Left faction, including Bordiga and Gramsci, lost influence, with Gramsci and Bordiga imprisoned on Ustica in 1926; Palmiro Togliatti was elected secretary in 1927. In 1930, Bordiga was expelled from the Comintern for Trotskyism. After Joseph Stalin dissolved the Comintern in 1943, exiled members in Moscow renamed the party the Italian Communist Party (PCI) on 15 May, reflecting a shift from international to national focus. The PCI was outlawed during the fascist regime but maintained a clandestine network, distributing propaganda, infiltrating fascist organizations, and playing a major role in the resistance movement against Mussolini, including leading a campaign against the Second Italo-Ethiopian War. After the fall of Fascism on 25 July 1943, the PCI returned to legal status and participated in the national liberation (Resistenza), forming partisan groups like the Garibaldi Brigades. In April 1944, after the Svolta di Salerno, Togliatti agreed to cooperate with King Victor Emmanuel III and Prime Minister Pietro Badoglio, and the PCI took part in every government from June 1944 to May 1947, contributing to the new Italian constitution, including the Gullo decrees. In the 1946 general election, the PCI gained nearly 19% of the vote, winning 104 seats in the Constituent Assembly, and the referendum that followed established a republic. In May 1947, amid political crisis following the Portella della Ginestra massacre, the United States pressured Alcide De Gasperi to remove the PCI and PSI from government, citing anti-communism as a condition for American aid. In the 1948 general election, the PCI joined the PSI in the Popular Democratic Front (FDP) but was defeated by Christian Democracy (DC), with the U.S. government spending $10–20 million on anti-communist propaganda and covert operations, including through the Marshall Plan. The British and American governments also obstructed justice for Italian war criminals. The PCI gained electoral success in the following years, particularly in Emilia-Romagna, Tuscany, and Umbria, and regularly won local elections, demonstrating effective, clean governance in cities like Bologna and Florence. After the 1975 local elections, the PCI was the strongest force in nearly all major municipal councils. The Soviet Union's suppression of the Hungarian Revolution in 1956 caused a split, with Togliatti and Giorgio Napolitano supporting the Soviet position in l'Unità, while Giuseppe Di Vittorio, Antonio Giolitti, and Pietro Nenni opposed it; Napolitano later expressed regret over his stance. In the mid-1960s, the U.S. estimated PCI membership at approximately 1.35 million (4.2% of the working-age population), making it the largest Communist party in per capita terms in the capitalist world and the largest in Western Europe, surpassing the Social Democratic Party of Germany. U.S. sources claimed the PCI received $40–50 million annually from the Soviets, though declassified information suggests this was exaggerated. Concerned about potential coups after the Athens Colonel coup in 1967, the PCI, led by Giorgio Amendola, requested Soviet assistance, and the KGB provided training in clandestine warfare and intelligence gathering to PCI members from 1967 to 1973, with members sent to East Germany and Moscow. Before the 1972 general election, PCI leader Longo personally requested and received an additional $5.7 million from Leonid Brezhnev, on top of $3.5 million received in 1971. The Soviets also provided further funding through other channels.

Former KGB archivist Vasili Mitrokhin, along with Longo and other PCI leaders, became concerned about the possibility of a coup in Italy following the Athens Colonel coup in April 1967, which established the Greek junta. These fears were not entirely baseless, as there had been two prior attempted coups in Italy: Piano Solo in 1964 and Golpe Borghese in 1970, carried out by military and neo-fascist groups. The PCI's Giorgio Amendola formally requested Soviet assistance to prepare the party for such an event. In response, the KGB developed and executed a plan to establish the PCI with its own intelligence and clandestine signal corps. From 1967 through 1973, PCI members were sent to East Germany and Moscow to receive training in clandestine warfare and information gathering from both the Stasi and the KGB. Shortly before the 1972 Italian general election, Longo personally wrote to Leonid Brezhnev, requesting and receiving an additional $5.7 million in funding, in addition to the $3.5 million the Soviet Union had provided to the PCI in 1971. The Soviets also supplied further funding through front organizations that offered generous contracts to PCI members. In 1969, Enrico Berlinguer, the PCI deputy national secretary and later secretary general, participated in the international conference of communist parties in Moscow, where his delegation opposed the official political line and refused to support the final report. Unexpectedly to his hosts, Berlinguer's speech challenged the communist leadership in Moscow, refusing to excommunicate the Chinese Communist Party and directly stating that the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia, which he called "the tragedy in Prague," revealed significant differences within the communist movement on issues such as national sovereignty, socialist democracy, and cultural freedom. At the time, the PCI, having absorbed the PSI's left-wing faction, the Italian Socialist Party of Proletarian Unity, had become the largest communist party in a capitalist country, winning 34.4% of the vote in the 1976 Italian general election. Relations between the PCI and the Soviet Union deteriorated in the 1970s and 1980s as the party distanced itself from Soviet obedience and Marxist–Leninist orthodoxy, moving instead toward Eurocommunism and the Socialist International. The PCI pursued a policy known as the Historic Compromise, seeking collaboration with socialist and Christian democratic parties. However, this effort ended after the kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro, the DC leader, by the Red Brigades in May 1978. The compromise was largely abandoned as a PCI policy in 1981. The Proletarian Unity Party merged into the PCI in 1984. During the Years of Lead, the PCI strongly opposed terrorism and the Red Brigades, who murdered or wounded many PCI members or trade unionists close to the party. According to Mitrokhin, the PCI asked the Soviets to pressure the StB, Czechoslovakia's State Security, to withdraw support for the group, but Moscow was either unable or unwilling to do so. This, combined with the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, led to a complete rupture with Moscow in 1979. In 1980, the PCI refused to attend the international conference of communist parties in Paris; cash payments to the PCI continued until 1984. Achille Occhetto became general secretary of the PCI in 1988. At a 1989 conference in a working-class section of Bologna, Occhetto delivered a speech announcing the Revolutions of 1989, now known in Italian politics as the svolta della Bolognina (Bolognina turning point). The collapse of communist governments in Eastern Europe led Occhetto to conclude that the era of Eurocommunism had ended. Under his leadership, the PCI dissolved and was refounded as the Democratic Party of the Left, which positioned itself as a progressive left-wing and democratic socialist party. A third of the PCI membership, led by Armando Cossutta, refused to join the PDS and instead formed the Communist Refoundation Party. Throughout its history, the PCI was especially strong in Central Italy, particularly in the Red Regions of Emilia-Romagna, Marche, Tuscany, and Umbria, as well as in Northern Italy's industrial cities. The party's most notable municipal achievement was Bologna, which remained under PCI control from 1945 onward. Among other initiatives, the local PCI administration implemented successful programs in elderly health, nursery education, and traffic reform, while also advancing housing and school meal provisions. From 1946 to 1956, the Communist city council constructed 31 nursery schools, 896 flats, and 9 schools. Health care improved significantly, street lighting was installed, new drains and municipal launderettes were built, and 8,000 children received subsidized school meals. In 1972, then-mayor Renato Zangheri introduced an innovative traffic plan with strict limits on private vehicles and a renewed focus on affordable public transport. Bologna's social services expanded throughout the early and mid-1970s, with the city center restored, centers for the mentally ill established to assist those released from closed psychiatric hospitals, training and employment opportunities provided for the handicapped, afternoon activities for schoolchildren made less mindless than traditional doposcuola, and full-day school programming helping working parents.
